title: Image-sensor 4T pixel gain cell reads 1,000-electron packets
idea: Box: buried-channel storage well (~1-2k e-) x transfer gate + floating-diffusion source follower borrowed from 4T image pixels x correlated-double-sampling column sensing x planar CMOS x Si x CIS fab flow. Full charge transfer onto a tiny floating diffusion gives ~100 uV/e- gain, so a small well replaces the 5 fF capacitor and is written back after read.
why: Escapes the capacitor charge wall (fact 1); buried-channel wells with CIS-grade dark current (few e-/s) extend retention 10-100x (fact 3); reuses existing CIS fab capacity.
note: CIS pinned wells give ~e-/s dark current; doubt is density (~1 um pixels) and transfer speed; CIS MPW demo feasible.

title: Image-sensor pinned-photodiode storage node with a transfer gate
idea: Adapted from the CMOS image sensor's pinned photodiode: store the bit as electrons in a fully depleted buried n-well capped by a p+ pinning layer, isolated from every Si/SiO2 interface, and move it to a floating diffusion through a transfer gate. A source follower reads it like a 4T pixel, so ~1-3k electrons suffice instead of ~30k.
why: Pinned photodiodes reach dark currents of a few electrons per second (~aA) at room temperature, ~10^4x below the 13 fA tail (fact 3); retention of seconds nearly removes refresh and the need for a 60-75:1 capacitor (fact 1), at 3-4 transistors per cell.
note: Pinned wells cut dark current hugely, but 3-4T pixel-like cells are far larger than 6F2; demoable on CIS MPW.

title: Banker's insured deposits: refresh-free banks for data with backups
idea: A banker guards insured deposits lightly because losses are covered. Pages with a valid copy elsewhere (model weights, page cache, read-only datasets) go into banks run with refresh off or at 1-4 s, protected by strong per-line detection codes; a detected error triggers a transparent refetch from flash, CXL or a remote replica instead of a crash.
why: Read-mostly AI weights are a large share of DRAM; dropping their refresh cuts refresh power and bandwidth 50-90% in those banks with only detection metadata added.
note: At 1-4 s many cells fail; refetch rate and detection overhead decide net gain.

title: Retention-DLTS fingerprints the defect species behind the leakage tail
idea: Treat a commodity DRAM as a billion-pixel deep-level transient spectrometer. Measure each weak cell's retention time against temperature (the Arrhenius slope gives trap energy) and against wordline/plate bias (the field-enhancement factor separates Poole-Frenkel, phonon-assisted tunneling and GIDL). Cluster the signatures across vendors and lots to name the dominant defect species (Fe-B, vacancy-oxygen, interface Pb centers).
why: Knowing which defect sets the 13 fA tail tells fabs which fix (gettering, passivation or field relief) buys the most refresh relief. A two-person lab with FPGA testers and thermal chambers can do it for <$500k in 18 months (fact 3).
note: Executable lab study; retention activation-energy studies exist, cross-vendor fingerprinting is the twist.

title: Ten people, one kernel module: retire weak pages, run 4x tREFI
idea: 10-person constraint: ship software plus a BIOS setting. A kernel module runs a retention test at 4x the refresh interval and retires the ~0.01-0.1% of 4 KB pages that fail (BadRAM-style memmap exclusion). It stores the compressed failing-page list in the DIMM's user-writable SPD bytes so the list travels with the module, then sets tREFI 4x longer.
why: Fact 3: cuts refresh energy ~75% and recovers ~8-15% of bandwidth for under 0.1% of capacity, on any server, with no new hardware.
note: BadRAM plus longer tREFI; VRT and data-pattern dependence need guardband.

title: Memory that rots on purpose: nanoimprinted foil for short-lived data
idea: Inverts 'memory must keep data until overwritten': roll-to-roll nanoimprint (~100 nm) 1T1C oxide-TFT arrays on metal foil with small leaky cells (1-10 ms retention, no refresh circuitry), laminate ~50 foils into a block, and let accelerators store only activations, gradients and KV pages consumed within the retention window, recomputing on rare loss.
why: Roll-to-roll layers cost ~$1-5/m2 versus ~$10,000/m2 for EUV DRAM wafers, so even at ~30x lower density it is ~100x cheaper per GB for transient data; trade-off: no long-term storage, ~100 ns-1 us access.
note: Ultra-cheap R2R layers for transient data; doubts: 100 nm R2R overlay, inter-foil interconnect, sub-µs access.

title: Cookie-cutter procedural data regenerated from seeds instead of stored
idea: Like stamping cookies from a cutter instead of storing them, replace stored tensors that are pseudo-random or structured (random projections, initializations, LoRA bases, positional tables, dropout masks) with seeds plus near-memory generators. These recreate each line at access time.
why: Zero refresh: data that is never stored never needs refresh. It also cuts the DRAM footprint and data-movement energy (fact 5) for that share of memory.

title: Deep-space LDPC pages: refresh at the 1% retention quantile
idea: CCSDS deep-space links decode reliably near 1e-2 raw BER. Store each 4 KB page as one LDPC codeword (~15% parity, decoder in the HBM base die or CXL controller) and set refresh where 1% of cells have decayed instead of where the last 1e-9 tail cell does; the median retention distribution is far longer than the tail, so the interval grows from 64 ms to ~1-2 s.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy and bandwidth loss fall ~15-30x and per-row profiling and VRT guardbands are no longer needed; costs ~15% parity and decode latency hidden behind page-granular access.
note: Extends Hi-ECC ideas to LDPC at 1% BER; page-granular access and decode latency are costs.

title: Heat is the wordline: thermally gated access with 1.5 eV activation
idea: Inverts 'access devices are gated by voltage': put an ionic or deep-trap hopping conductor with ~1.5 eV activation energy in series with each capacitor, effectively insulating at 25 C (retention far beyond hours) while a nanosecond pulse in a row heater line takes it to ~400 C, raising conductance ~10^10x long enough to read or write; cells form 2-terminal crossbar stacks.
why: Two-terminal low-mask crossbar with refresh-free retention, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: heater energy per row access, thermal crosstalk, ~100 ns cycle.
note: 1.5 eV activation gives ~1e14 on/off between 25 and 400 C; doubts: heater energy, thermal crosstalk, dielectric leakage when hot.

title: Unified charge-debt counter for retention and row hammer
idea: Each row carries one counter that accumulates time weighted by temperature plus neighbor activations weighted by coupling. A row is refreshed when its debt crosses a threshold, so one mechanism handles both retention and hammer.
why: Replaces the fixed 64 ms sweep plus separate TRR. Quiet rows refresh 4-8x less often, and hammer victims (fact 9, ~1k ACTs) are restored exactly in time.
note: Per-row counters cost area; neat merge of retention and TRR.

title: Vertical charge-coupled memory: no switch per bit, just moving charge
idea: Inverts 'every bit needs its own access transistor': deposit a 200-layer gate/oxide stack (NAND-style, one hole etch), line each hole with a poly-Si or oxide channel, and clock the layer gates in 3 phases so charge packets march along the hole like a vertical CCD. Each hole holds ~60 bits and one sense/regeneration stage at the top restores packets as they circulate, so refresh is continuous and free.
why: No per-bit transistor, capacitor or litho: cost tracks 3D NAND (~$0.05-0.1/GB), ~100x below DRAM per GB; trade-off is serial access (~us to the far bit, high streaming bandwidth) and transfer-loss risk in poly channels.
note: CCD clocking in a NAND-style stack removes per-bit transistors and capacitors; poly-channel transfer efficiency and serial latency are the doubts.

title: Colors pick the layer: wavelength-addressed 3D stacks without staircases
idea: Inverts 'each 3D tier needs its own wired wordline contact': give each tier a photoconductive access element made of quantum dots tuned to a distinct absorption band (16 tiers, 16 wavelengths) and run a light pipe per column, so choosing the wavelength selects the tier and all tiers share their electrical lines with no staircase or tier-specific masks.
why: Removes staircase etch and per-tier wiring (fact 2), allowing 16-64 tiers at single-tier mask count, ~100x cheaper per GB; trade-off: optical crosstalk, us-class access, dot stability.
note: Removes staircase/per-tier wiring if 16-band QD photoswitches work; crosstalk, dot stability and slow optical access are big doubts.
